subject: Geography
title: Oceans and Seas
learningOutcomes: Differentiate between oceans and seas and name the world's five oceans.
Trace the movement of water through the river system and the hydrological cycle.
Evaluate the economic and strategic importance of oceans, marine biodiversity, and the Arabian Sea for Pakistan.
Identify and compare coastal and marine landforms such as islands, peninsulas, bays, gulfs, isthmuses, and straits.
Explain the causes of earthquakes, the stages of the rock cycle, and the main types of mineral resources.

sections.heading: Oceans and Seas
sections.body: About 70% of the Earth's surface is covered with water, which is why Earth is called the Blue Planet. Seas and oceans together hold 95% of all water on Earth; the remaining 5% is freshwater in glaciers, rivers, lakes, and underground. There are five oceans — Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic — and around fifty seas. Oceans are larger and deeper than seas and lie between continents, while seas are where the oceans meet the land and are mostly partially enclosed. The Caspian Sea is unique because it is enclosed by land on all sides.

sections.heading: The Five Oceans
sections.body: From largest to smallest by area, the oceans are the Pacific (165 M km²), Atlantic (106 M km²), Indian (70 M km²), Southern (20 M km²), and Arctic (14 M km²). Each has a deepest point: the Mariana Trench in the Pacific (10,924 m) is the deepest known point on Earth, followed by the Puerto Rico Trench (Atlantic), Java Trench (Indian), South Sandwich Trench (Southern), and Fram Basin (Arctic). The Pacific is the deepest on average, while the Arctic is both the smallest and the shallowest.

sections.heading: Rivers and the Water Cycle
sections.body: A river begins at its source (headwaters) and ends at its mouth. Along the way it is fed by tributaries, may loop into meanders, and can deposit sediment as a fan-shaped delta. A river with all its tributaries is a river system, also called a drainage basin. The hydrological cycle, or water cycle, continuously moves water between Earth and the atmosphere through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff, and infiltration, replenishing the freshwater that life depends on.

sections.heading: Why Oceans Matter
sections.body: Oceans produce over 50% of the world's oxygen — mostly through marine phytoplankton — and store about 50 times more carbon dioxide than the atmosphere, helping regulate climate by carrying heat from the equator to the poles. They provide food, medicines, jobs, recreation, and trade routes. Marine biodiversity includes around 500,000 known species, with the true total estimated as high as 10 million. For Pakistan, the Arabian Sea carries 95% of total trade and 100% of petroleum, lubricants, and oil, making it vital to the economy.

sections.heading: Features of the Sea
sections.body: An island is surrounded by water on all sides (continental like Greenland, or oceanic like Hawaii). A peninsula is surrounded by water on three sides and joined to the mainland on one. A bay is surrounded by land on three sides with a wide opening; a gulf penetrates deep into the land with a narrow mouth. An isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining two landmasses (Panama, Suez), while a strait is a narrow strip of water joining two water bodies (Gibraltar, Hormuz).

sections.heading: Earthquakes, Rocks, and Minerals
sections.body: Earthquakes are the shaking of the Earth when tectonic plates move at fault lines; the focus is where they start underground and the epicenter is the point directly above on the surface. The rock cycle continuously recycles rock between igneous (cooled magma or lava), sedimentary (compressed sediment), and metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure) forms. Mineral resources are classified as metallic (iron, bauxite), non-metallic (limestone, gypsum), and energy minerals (coal, petroleum), the last of which are non-renewable fossil fuels.

definitions.definition: An enormous mass of saltwater between continents; larger and deeper than a sea.
A smaller, shallower body of saltwater where the ocean meets the land, mostly partially enclosed.
A smaller river or stream that flows into a larger river.
Fan-shaped land formed at a river's mouth by deposited sediment.
The continuous movement of water between the Earth and its atmosphere.
The rising of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface.
A narrow strip of land connecting two landmasses and separating two water bodies.
A narrow strip of water connecting two larger water bodies.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's focus.
The continuous process by which rocks are recycled from one type to another.

examTips: Fix the order of the water cycle: Evaporation → Transpiration → Condensation → Precipitation → Surface runoff → Infiltration.
Don't mix up an isthmus (narrow strip of LAND) with a strait (narrow strip of WATER) — this is commonly tested.
Learn the five oceans by size (Pacific → Atlantic → Indian → Southern → Arctic) and each ocean's deepest trench.
